introduction: The first of these readings is about an infant: before it could ask for anything, a mother and her milk were ready. From that picture of a mercy that precedes asking the readings widen to a bounty shed on all creatures as sunlight is, a Day of Grace and not of Justice, forgiveness that grows as rebellion grows, and prayers that cling to the cord of mercy. The Psalms, Isaiah, the parables of Jesus, Paul on grace, the Qur’an’s “My mercy embraceth all things”, Saʿdī and Shakespeare’s Portia and Isabella say much of this in their own voices. The harder questions are here too. Tennyson sets nature’s cruelty against the creed; Confucius would repay injury with justice; the elder brother and Jonah resent the pardon of others; Paul asks why God still finds fault and whether one may sin so that grace may abound; the Mishnah holds that no day of atonement covers a wrong done to a neighbour; and the Dhammapada says that no one can purify another.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá distinguishes a mercy that precedes asking from one that follows supplication. Which of the outside passages speak of the first and which of the second, and why might both be needed?

Justice gives each his due; bounty rewards one who has done no work. Hear the labourers who worked all day, the elder brother and Confucius. What is right in their protest, and how do the readings answer it?
“As mine iniquities waxed greater and greater, Thy forbearance towards me augmented.” Paul asks whether we should then continue in sin. What in the readings prevents that conclusion?

The readings speak of a Night on which all trespasses are forgiven; the Mishnah says that a wrong done to another person is not atoned for until that person is pacified; Jesus ties being forgiven to forgiving. How do divine pardon and what people owe one another fit together?

Macbeth is sure that an ocean will not clean his hand, and Khayyám that no tears wash out a word; the readings say that one gleam blots out every trace. What is the difference between these speakers that leads them to such different certainties?
The Dhammapada teaches that one is purified by oneself and by no other. What does that teaching guard, and what do these prayers for forgiveness guard that it leaves out?

outside.why: Before the infant “ever asks for it”, mother and milk are prepared: “a pure gift out of grace”. The First Epistle of John puts the order in eight words: we love him, because he first loved us.
Grace and mercy “have preceded us from every direction”. Paul dates the love of God in the same way, before any deserving: while we were yet sinners.
“This is the bounty of the Beloved that He hath bestowed before any request.” Julian of Norwich hears that even the asking is given: I am Ground of thy beseeching.

“He bestowed existence and granted being”, and ordained the means by which the world is ordered. Paul tells a pagan crowd that God never left himself without witness: rain from heaven, fruitful seasons, food and gladness.
“The Mercy of the infinite God is shed on all creatures.” The psalm: the Lord is good to all, and his tender mercies are over all his works.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá sees mercy shed on every creature as sunlight is. Tennyson, with the fossil record before him, saw Nature “red in tooth and claw” shrieking against the creed that God is love. What does each of them count as evidence?

This is the saying ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes. In the Gospel the rain on the just and the unjust is given as the reason for loving one’s enemies; the reading draws from it that “the mercy of God is universal”.
“It is a mercy which precedes asking.” Isaiah has the promise in those terms: before they call, I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear.
“Poor are we, yet the outpouring of the treasury of the Kingdom is boundless.” Paul turns the same fact against boasting: what hast thou that thou didst not receive?
“Thy mercy hath surpassed all created things.” In the Qur’an God answers Moses’ prayer in these words: My mercy embraceth all things.

“He Whose mercy hath encompassed all the worlds.” The Qur’an gives the phrase to those who bear the Throne, as they ask forgiveness for those on earth: Thou comprehendest all things in mercy and knowledge.
“Look not upon the people and the things they possess; look rather upon the wonders of Thy gifts.” Daniel prays on the same ground: not for our righteousnesses, but for thy great mercies.
“Not for a moment hath His grace been withheld.” The poet of Lamentations says it in a destroyed city: his compassions fail not; they are new every morning.
God is called “the Concealer of their sins”. The psalm blesses the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered.
“The Sovereign Protector of all men, and the Concealer of their sins.” Saʿdī opens the Gulistān on the same attribute: He tears not the veil of reputation of His worshippers even for grievous sins.
“Be then of good cheer … all the trespasses committed by the people of the earth have been forgiven.” Isaiah is told to speak so to Jerusalem: her iniquity is pardoned.

On this Night every trespass is forgiven. The Mishnah, speaking of its own day of forgiveness, makes one exception: what one has done to a fellow is not atoned for until the fellow has been pacified. Does a general pardon reach the wrongs people have done to each other?
“He has always chosen certain souls upon whom He has shed the Divine Bounty of His heart.” To Moses, asking to see the glory: I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious.
Certain souls are chosen. Paul states the choice at its hardest, and voices the question it raises: why doth he yet find fault? The reading does not ask it. What does it say that bears on it?
A bounty conferred “for which the mighty ones of bygone ages had craved in vain”. Jesus to his disciples: many prophets and righteous men have desired to see those things which ye see.
“I am the one … who lay fast asleep on his couch, when lo, the messengers of Thy manifold mercies were sent down upon me.” Thompson did more than sleep: he fled, and was followed.
“Is there any giver save God?” James: every good gift and every perfect gift is from above.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s example is a workman and his wage: justice pays what is due, “bounty consists in rewarding him even when he has done no work”. Jesus tells it as a story, with the complaint of those who worked all day.
“Christ besought forgiveness for those responsible for His death: This is called bounty.” These are the words.
Justice renders to each his due; bounty goes beyond it. Hamlet corrects Polonius on the treatment of the players: use every man after his desert, and who should ’scape whipping?

The reading sets bounty above justice, with forgiveness of one’s killers as the example. Asked whether injury should be repaid with kindness, Confucius asks what then is left to repay kindness with, and answers: injury with justice. What would be lost in a world that ran only on bounty?

“The veiled soul who is endowed with good character and conduct merits the forgiveness of God.” Paul’s letter denies merit any part: by grace are ye saved, not of works, lest any man should boast. Does the reading mean by merit what Paul rules out?
The reading explains a deprivation that is “equivalent to the denial of divine forgiveness”: failing to partake of the outpourings of the Holy Spirit. The saying being explained is this one.
“This is not the Day of Justice but the Day of Grace.” James: mercy rejoiceth against judgment.

“Look thou not at the degree of thy capacity, look thou at the boundless favour.” The elder brother in the parable has looked at capacity and service all his life, and his protest at the feast is never answered by himself. What does grace owe to those who kept the rules?

“He sendeth down mercy upon whomsoever He willeth and withholdeth mercy from whomsoever He willeth.” FitzGerald’s Khayyám turns that sovereignty into an accusation, and offers forgiveness in the other direction. What in the reading answers him?
The Báb’s sentence follows this verse of the Qur’an almost word for word: one thing is not forgiven, and anything else is, to whom He will.
“God transforms evil deeds into good deeds through His grace.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá is citing the Qur’an, where the promise is made to one who repents, believes and does righteous work.

“If Thou shouldst will by the decree of justice, all who dwell in the kingdoms of the heavens and earth would perish in an instant.” The Qur’an: were Allah to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave on earth a living creature.

The Báb says that by justice alone none would survive, and that God’s custom is pardon. The psalm from the depths: if thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities, who shall stand? But there is forgiveness with thee.
“As mine iniquities waxed greater and greater, Thy forbearance towards me augmented.” Paul: where sin abounded, grace did much more abound.

If forbearance grows with rebellion, why stop? Paul sees the inference at once and refuses it: shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. The reading’s own answer is in its first words: “O misery, misery!”
“One gleam from the splendors of Thy Name, the All-Merciful, sufficeth to banish and blot out every trace of sinfulness.” Isaiah: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.

One gleam is enough to blot out every trace. Macbeth, a few minutes after the murder, is sure of the opposite: the whole ocean will not wash his hand; his hand will redden the sea. What does he lack that the speaker of the reading has?
“How farsoever they may have strayed from Thee … yet Thou, in Thine essence, art the All-Bountiful.” The father in the parable sees his son while he is yet a great way off, and runs.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls faith “the fountain of Job” and quotes this verse: the spring that rose under Job’s foot, to wash in and to drink.
“Faith is the cause of forgiveness.” Paul’s conclusion, on which the Reformation turned: a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
“Today the ocean of mercy is surging.” The Qur’an’s widest invitation is addressed to those who have been prodigal to their own hurt: despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins.
“Fear God, then return unto Him … Repent unto God Who created thee.” Isaiah: let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy; for he will abundantly pardon.
“God hath forgiven what is past.” The psalm measures how far the past is put away: as far as the east is from the west.
“Thy forgiveness hath preceded sin.” The Qur’an says that the Lord has prescribed mercy for Himself, so that whoever does evil in ignorance and then repents finds Him forgiving.
“Blessed art thou for having confessed before the Throne, and He hath, through His grace, absolved thee.” The First Epistle of John: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive.

God has forgiven those who did what was forbidden, and they are told to fear God and act on His command. The woman taken in adultery hears both sentences together: neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.

“Look ye not upon the purity or impurity of his nature: look ye upon the all-embracing mercy of the Lord.” Luke’s version of the command gives the same reason: he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil.
“Stranger and friend alike are seated at the table of His favor.” It was said of Jesus as a reproach that he kept such a table: a friend of publicans and sinners.
This is the verse ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes: both these and those are supplied from the bounty of the Lord, and it is not walled up from anyone.
“He sees fault yet bestows gifts, finds sin yet grants shelter.” The psalm gives the reason a father would: he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust.

“All created things are prone to error and ever shall be”, and God’s gaze is on the goodly deeds. Pope’s line divides the same two things between the same two parties: to err is human; to forgive, divine.

God’s gaze, says the reading, “is fixed upon the goodly deeds of souls who have turned to Him”. Jesus looks at a woman his host sees only as a sinner: her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much.
This is the story ‘Abdu’l-Bahá tells, as Benjamin Franklin retold it in the style of Genesis; it comes from Saʿdī. Franklin’s God has borne with the idolater a hundred ninety and eight years.
“For a hundred years this man has been an idol worshipper and I have been patient with him.” The Second Letter of Peter reads every delay that way: longsuffering, not willing that any should perish.

Abraham could not bear the idolater for one night. Jonah could not bear the pardon of Nineveh, and says why he fled: I knew that thou art a gracious God. Why is another’s mercy so hard on the religious?
“This Day a door is open wider than both heaven and earth.” The Epistle to the Hebrews draws the practical conclusion: let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace.
“Do Thou be forbearing toward them.” The Qur’an counts among the good those who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind.
“Neither do Thou lay hold on them for the things they have committed in Thy days.” Peter asks how often he must forgive, and offers seven times.

The disturbed “must be treated with conciliation”, for “most souls are weak”. Isaiah’s servant is known by the same gentleness: a bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench.
“If He loved them not, He would have created them not.” The Wisdom of Solomon argues in the same way: never wouldest thou have made any thing, if thou hadst hated it.
“All mankind is but one fold and God, the Kindly Shepherd.” In John the one fold is still to come: other sheep I have, which are not of this fold.

“The sustenances provided for man are blessings. Sight, hearing and all his faculties are wonderful gifts.” Charles Lamb wanted a grace said for more than dinner: for a walk, a meeting with a friend, a book.
“He has provided our foods, drink and other requirements.” Deuteronomy warns the prosperous against the one sentence that undoes this: my power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth.
“The heavenly table is set.” The psalm: thou preparest a table before me; my cup runneth over.
“Strive ye to receive your share of this eternal food.” Isaiah cries the invitation in a market: come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
“With a nod He layeth balm on every wound, with a glimpse He freeth the hearts from the shackles of grief.” Jesus: come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
“The Almighty will no doubt grant you the help of His grace.” Paul, refused what he asked for, was told that the grace was enough: my strength is made perfect in weakness.
A delay that felt like prison “hath been a divine gift”. Paul’s confidence is general: all things work together for good to them that love God.
The signs “have encompassed the world”, yet the ignorant “appear heedless, nay rather, rebellious”. Ten lepers are healed on the road and one turns back.
“Affliction is but mercy, and grief a gift from God.” The Epistle to the Hebrews reads suffering as a father’s hand: whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks a sufferer to praise God for a “dire affliction, which is but bounty unalloyed”. Leonato, grieving, will take no such counsel from men who are not in pain: there was never yet philosopher that could endure the toothache patiently. Who may say to another that grief is a gift?
“With every fleeting breath, grant her the blessing of Thy bounty.” Saʿdī counts two blessings in every breath, the drawing in and the letting out, and a thanks due for each.
The suppliant waits “at the door of Thy bounty”. In a saying of Muḥammad, God describes how the distance is closed from the other side: if he comes to Me walking, I go to him running.
“The cord of Thy mercy which hath surpassed the entire creation.” Micah ends his book asking who is a God like this, who retains not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy.
“Do Thou have mercy upon the bearer of this Tablet.” The oldest blessing in the Bible asks the same for the one who receives it: the Lord make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee.

The prayer calls on the Name through which loving-kindness was shed and wickedness abolished. The name proclaimed to Moses holds both: merciful and gracious, forgiving iniquity, “and that will by no means clear the guilty”. How do these readings hold the second clause?
“Do with them, therefore, as becometh Thy mercy.” David, offered a choice of punishments, chooses on the same reckoning: let us fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercies are great.
The prayer asks that hardship be transformed “into comfort and tranquility”. The Qur’an gives the assurance twice over: with hardship goeth ease.
“The best among us will need that grace and mercy.” Isabella to a judge who thinks himself beyond need of it: all the souls that were were forfeit once.
The best will need mercy “and will find it joyfully awaiting him”. Of the two men who went up to the temple to pray, the one who asked only for mercy went home justified.
“Forgive me my sins, and pardon me my trespasses.” The great penitential psalm asks on the only ground it has: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies.
“Sick am I; heal me … Forgive me my sins.” The Dhammapada knows no such request: by oneself the evil is done, by oneself one is purified; no one can purify another. What is each tradition protecting?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá raises his hands for a handmaiden who has died. Abraham in the Qur’an prays in the same way for others: forgive me and my parents and believers on the day when the account is cast.
“Whose pardon and generosity are all-embracing.” Portia: the quality of mercy is not strained; it droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven.

“O Thou Whose mercy hath encompassed all, Whose forgiveness is transcendent.” Donne tests the reach of it sin by sin, and keeps finding one more: when thou hast done, thou hast not done, for I have more.

“Make them the signs of Thy forgiveness and the manifestations of Thy forbearance.” The Sermon on the Mount makes it a condition: if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours. Is being forgiven complete before one forgives?
To be a sign of God’s forgiveness is to forgive. The Qur’an asks it of those who had cause for grievance: let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you?

“Thou hast lifted to these parched lips the living waters of Thy loving-kindness and revived this weary and withered soul.” Isaiah: in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert.
“Thou art He Who from everlasting hath succored whosoever hath sought Thee.” The Qur’an: I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me.
“Cast not out … them that have sought Thee.” In Ezekiel God takes the seeking on Himself: I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away.
“Withhold not from me Thy grace, for Thee alone do I seek.” Augustine: my whole hope is only in Your exceeding great mercy.

The prayer trusts that the door will not be shut. Khayyám’s most quoted stanza allows no appeal: the Moving Finger writes, and neither piety nor tears will wash out a word of it. Is what is done ever undone, on the readings’ account, or is something else changed?
“If Thou ceasest to be merciful unto Thy servants, who, then, will show mercy unto them?” Peter, asked whether he too will leave: Lord, to whom shall we go?

The prayer pleads that there is no one else to turn to. Abraham pleads for Sodom differently, holding God to His own standard: shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? Is mercy asked as a favour or claimed as what befits the giver?
“Enable him then to seek shelter beneath the shadow of Thy most exalted Name.” The psalm: he that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.

The prayer would gather God’s servants “beneath the shade of the Tree of Thy gracious providence”, among its leaves and its singing Bird. The kingdom in the parable is such a tree, with the birds of the air lodging in its branches.

“Suffer them not to be kept back from the shores of the ocean of Thy nearness.” Ezekiel hears the will that lies behind such a prayer: I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; turn ye, for why will ye die?
“Nourish me from the Table Thou didst send down out of the clouds of Thy bounty.” Jesus in the Qur’an asks for a table spread with food from heaven, to be a feast and a sign.

psalm-as-far-as-the-east.text: The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy. He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever. He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities. For as the heaven is high above the earth, so great is his mercy toward them that fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us

psalm-remembereth-we-are-dust.text: Like as a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth them that fear him. For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust

psalm-tender-mercies-over-all.text: The Lord is gracious, and full of compassion; slow to anger, and of great mercy. The Lord is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works

psalm-openest-thine-hand.text: The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season. Thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing

psalm-who-shall-stand.text: If thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared

psalm-have-mercy-upon-me.text: Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions. Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me

psalm-transgression-forgiven.text: Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man unto whom the Lord imputeth not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile

psalm-table-before-me.text: Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over. Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the Lord for ever

exodus-merciful-and-gracious.text: The Lord, The Lord God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty

exodus-gracious-to-whom.text: I will make all my goodness pass before thee, and I will proclaim the name of the Lord before thee; and will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will shew mercy on whom I will shew mercy

romans-whom-he-will.text: Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth. Thou wilt say then unto me, Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will? Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus

isaiah-sins-as-scarlet.text: Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool

isaiah-abundantly-pardon.text: Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon

isaiah-can-a-woman-forget.text: Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee

isaiah-before-they-call.text: And it shall come to pass, that before they call, I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear

micah-delighteth-in-mercy.text: Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy. He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea

luke-prodigal-a-great-way-off.text: And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. And the son said unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son. But the father said to his servants, Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet

luke-elder-brother.text: Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment: and yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends: But as soon as this thy son was come, which hath devoured thy living with harlots, thou hast killed for him the fatted calf. And he said unto him, Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine. It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found

matthew-labourers-in-the-vineyard.text: These last have wrought but one hour, and thou hast made them equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day. But he answered one of them, and said, Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny? Take that thine is, and go thy way: I will give unto this last, even as unto thee. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good

luke-kind-unto-the-unthankful.text: But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil. Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful

luke-loved-much.text: Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little

luke-publican.text: And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted

matthew-if-ye-forgive-not.text: For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses

matthew-blasphemy-not-forgiven.text: All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men: but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men

matthew-good-gifts.text: Or what man is there of you, whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone? Or if he ask a fish, will he give him a serpent? If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him

romans-while-yet-sinners.text: But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us

romans-grace-did-much-more-abound.text: Moreover the law entered, that the offence might abound. But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound

romans-continue-in-sin.text: What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein

john-epistle-confess-our-sins.text: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness

john-epistle-first-loved-us.text: We love him, because he first loved us

james-every-good-gift.text: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning

james-mercy-rejoiceth.text: For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment

corinthians-didst-not-receive.text: For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it

corinthians-by-the-grace-of-god.text: For I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me

hebrews-throne-of-grace.text: Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need

ezekiel-no-pleasure.text: As I live, saith the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel

peter-not-willing-any-perish.text: The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance

genesis-judge-of-all-the-earth.text: And Abraham drew near, and said, Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked? Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city: wilt thou also destroy and not spare the place for the fifty righteous that are therein? That be far from thee to do after this manner, to slay the righteous with the wicked: and that the righteous should be as the wicked, that be far from thee: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right

john-neither-do-i-condemn.text: He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her. And again he stooped down, and wrote on the ground. And they which heard it, being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, even unto the last: and Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst. When Jesus had lifted up himself, and saw none but the woman, he said unto her, Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee? She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more

samuel-hand-of-the-lord.text: And David said unto Gad, I am in a great strait: let us fall now into the hand of the Lord; for his mercies are great: and let me not fall into the hand of man

deuteronomy-power-to-get-wealth.text: And thou say in thine heart, My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth. But thou shalt remember the Lord thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth

acts-rain-from-heaven.text: Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness

daniel-not-for-our-righteousnesses.text: for we do not present our supplications before thee for our righteousnesses, but for thy great mercies

quran-despair-not-of-mercy.text: Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt! Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins. Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.

quran-mercy-embraceth-all.text: And ordain for us in this world that which is good, and in the Hereafter (that which is good), Lo! We have turned unto Thee. He said: I smite with My punishment whom I will, and My mercy embraceth all things, therefore I shall ordain it for those who ward off (evil) and pay the poor-due, and those who believe Our revelations;

quran-prescribed-for-himself-mercy.text: And when those who believe in Our revelations come unto thee, say: Peace be unto you! Your Lord hath prescribed for Himself mercy, that whoso of you doeth evil through ignorance and repenteth afterward thereof and doeth right, (for him) lo! He is Forgiving, Merciful.

quran-forgiveth-not-partners.text: Lo! Allah forgiveth not that a partner should be ascribed unto Him. He forgiveth (all) save that to whom He will. Whoso ascribeth partners to Allah, he hath indeed invented a tremendous sin.

quran-these-and-those.text: Each do We supply, both these and those, from the bounty of thy Lord. And the bounty of thy Lord can never be walled up.

quran-evil-deeds-to-good.text: Save him who repenteth and believeth and doth righteous work; as for such, Allah will change their evil deeds to good deeds. Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful.

quran-cool-bath.text: (And it was said unto him): Strike the ground with thy foot. This (spring) is a cool bath and a refreshing drink.

quran-cannot-reckon.text: And if ye would count the favour of Allah ye cannot reckon it. Lo! Allah is indeed Forgiving, Merciful.

quran-take-mankind-to-task.text: If Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrong-doing, he would not leave hereon a living creature, but He reprieveth them to an appointed term, and when their term cometh they cannot put (it) off an hour nor (yet) advance (it).

quran-comprehendest-in-mercy.text: Those who bear the Throne, and all who are round about it, hymn the praises of their Lord and believe in Him and ask forgiveness for those who believe (saying): Our Lord! Thou comprehendest all things in mercy and knowledge, therefor forgive those who repent and follow Thy way. Ward off from them the punishment of hell.

quran-yearn-ye-not.text: And let not those who possess dignity and ease among you swear not to give to the near of kin and to the needy, and to fugitives for the cause of Allah. Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you? Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.

quran-mercy-for-the-peoples.text: We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples.

quran-which-favours-deny.text: Which is it, of the favours of your Lord, that ye deny?

jonah-angry-at-mercy.text: But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry. And he prayed unto the Lord, and said, I pray thee, O Lord, was not this my saying, when I was yet in my country? Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil

shakespeare-after-his-desert.text: use every man / after his desert, and who should 'scape whipping? / Use them after your own honour and dignity: the less / they deserve, the more merit is in your bounty
shakespeare-after-his-desert.author: William Shakespeare

shakespeare-forfeit-once.text: Why, all the souls that were were forfeit once; / And He that might the vantage best have took / Found out the remedy. How would you be, / If He, which is the top of judgment, should / But judge you as you are? O, think on that; / And mercy then will breathe within your lips, / Like man new made
shakespeare-forfeit-once.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-course-of-justice.text: Though justice be thy plea, consider this, / That, in the course of justice, none of us / Should see salvation: we do pray for mercy; / And that same prayer doth teach us all to render / The deeds of mercy
shakespeare-course-of-justice.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-neptunes-ocean.text: Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather / The multitudinous seas in incarnadine, / Making the green one red
shakespeare-neptunes-ocean.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

saadi-veil-of-reputation.text: The showers of his boundless mercy have penetrated to every spot, and the banquet of his unstinted liberality is spread out everywhere. He tears not the veil of reputation of his worshippers even for grievous sins, and does not withhold their daily allowance of bread for great crimes
saadi-veil-of-reputation.author: Saʿdī

mishnah-pacified-his-fellow.text: for transgressions between man and God Yom HaKippurim effects atonement, but for transgressions between man and his fellow Yom HaKippurim does not effect atonement, until he has pacified his fellow

avot-judged-with-goodness.text: Everything is foreseen yet freedom of choice is granted, And the world is judged with goodness; And everything is in accordance with the preponderance of works

donne-wilt-thou-forgive.text: Wilt thou forgive that sin where I begun, / Which is my sin, though it were done before? / Wilt thou forgive that sin through which I run, / And do run still, though still I do deplore? / When thou hast done, thou hast not done, / For I have more
donne-wilt-thou-forgive.author: John Donne
donne-wilt-thou-forgive.work: A Hymn to God the Father

thompson-hound-of-heaven.text: I fled Him, down the nights and down the days; / I fled Him, down the arches of the years; / I fled Him, down the labyrinthine ways / Of my own mind; and in the mist of tears / I hid from Him, and under running laughter. / Up vistaed hopes I sped; / And shot, precipitated / Adown Titanic glooms of chasmed fears, / From those strong Feet that followed, followed after
thompson-hound-of-heaven.author: Francis Thompson

khayyam-forgiveness-give-and-take.text: Oh Thou, who Man of baser Earth didst make, / And ev'n with Paradise devise the Snake: / For all the Sin wherewith the Face of Man / Is blacken'd—Man's forgiveness give—and take!
khayyam-forgiveness-give-and-take.author: Omar Khayyám
khayyam-forgiveness-give-and-take.caveat: FitzGerald’s version is a free adaptation; this stanza has no close original in the Persian.

franklin-parable-against-persecution.text: And God said, Have I born with him these hundred ninety and eight Years, and nourished him, and cloathed him, notwithstanding his Rebellion against me, and couldst not thou, that art thyself a Sinner, bear with him one Night?
franklin-parable-against-persecution.author: Benjamin Franklin
franklin-parable-against-persecution.currency: Franklin retold an old Eastern story, found in Saʿdī’s Būstān, in the style of Genesis.
